newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - Nov 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - Nov 26.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- WEN WEI PO -- Chinese President Jiang Zemin announced at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum that China would cut its average tariff rate from around 23 percent to 15 percent towards 2000.
-- Chinese Vice-Premier Qian Qichen said China and the United States had agreed that China would join the World Trade Organisation before the exchange of presidential visits.

-- APPLE DAILY -- Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping's youngest son-in-law had not lost his title as deputy managing director of a major Chinese group as rumours suggested after the exposure of the smuggling of 2,000 A-47 guns to the United States. It said he still held his position in the army, which showed there was still a powerful force at the top protecting the Deng family.
-- MING PAO -- Jiang promised that mainland Chinese would not rush to Hong Kong after the handover during a meeting with the territory's Financial Secretary Donald Tsang in Manila.
-- Ninety percent of Chinese university students could not name 10 foreign literary masterpieces and most of them had not read traditional Chinese classics such as the works of Confucius and Sun Zi.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Canada was to sign an agreement with China on Tuesday to provide US$1.5 billion in loans for building two nuclear reactors in Zhejiang province in its biggest commercial deal on the mainland.
-- International reinsurance groups are scambling for a foothold in China's market despite its present small size.
-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Development Bank of Singapore was reorienting its Hong Kong operations to be the centre of its strategic thrust into China.

-- China had given new hints that its three-year austerity programme was over, pronouncing its anti-inflation battle a success and saying that its new task was ensuring stability as the nation prepares to recover Hong Kong.
